newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Credit Lyonnais faces tough EU talks.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais faces tough EU talks.

text.p: The European Commission, about to receive a French request to rescue Credit Lyonnais for the third time in four years, said on Thursday it would impose tough conditions, including further asset disposals, on any new state subsidies.

"Assets will have to be sold, there is not a shadow of a doubt about that. There will be conditions and they will be tougher; nothing could be more logical," a spokesman for European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said.
He was reacting to a flood of questions from reporters eager to hear about the new plan expected to reach the Commission this week.
The spokesman said he did not know how much more money the French state was proposing to inject into the state-owned bank to ready it for privatisation.

But taking into account some nine billion francs ($1.6 billion) in losses from the selling of assets, imposed by the Commission in 1995, and 3.9 billion francs in emergency aid agreed last year, the bank would need no less than 19-20 billion francs, he speculated. He declined to elaborate.
French newspapers have reported that Lyonnais will need a total 30 billion francs.
The French government announced that it would file the new Lyonnais plan with the Commission this week. But the spokesman said it had not arrived on Thursday morning.
It will be the third time since 1994 that the French government has bailed out Lyonnais, once Europe's largest bank.

In 1995, the Commission approved a three-year restructuring programme involving a total of 45 billion francs in state subsidies. The plan consisted mainly of ridding the bank of some 130 billion francs in loss-making assets.

In return, the Commission imposed the condition that the bank should sell off at least 35 percent of its foreign assets by 1998 including a substantial part of its European banking network. It is unclear how much of this has been achieved.
Van Miert warned in October, when the Commission agreed to the emergency aid, that he would be looking for further divestments which should be "real and substantial".
The French state first rescued Credit Lyonnais in 1994 after the bank came to the brink of bankruptcy due to reckless expansion in the second half of the 80s. ($ = 5.699 French Francs)
